cells.tense: You know what to let go of here, and you are letting go of it on purpose.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Work a piece of this practice by hand for a season, without fixing anything, and notice what it asks of you as the months go.
cells.core:
You can carry something handed down without gripping it. When a custom or a way of doing things has run its course, you put it down cleanly, and the people doing it with you can feel you mean it. That's rare, and it's the whole reason what you carry stays alive rather than turning into furniture.

So spend a season with one piece of it, hands on the work, no verdict waiting at the end. Take the practice you've kept the longest — the one you might be running on habit — and handle it slowly. Be the one learning it rather than the one running it. Part of it will ask to change, and part will ask to stay exactly as it is. Both are answers, and you don't have to decide in advance which one wins. Whatever it turns into is still yours to pass on, and it will be more yours than it was.
cells.sheetLine: You can let a custom go without losing what it carried.
cells.verb: carrying a body of practice by hand, at whatever it now asks
cells.place: in the shared meaning and the customs that carry it, where it is kept or dropped

cells.tense: You are guarding the tradition against a change that has not arrived yet.
cells.act: put the inquiry on paper and follow it
cells.ask: Get one worry about how this practice might change onto a single page in plain order, then do only the next thing that page asks.
cells.core:
There's a way here that you keep alive, and lately you've been defending it against things that haven't happened. Every possible drift gets pre-empted, every new version gets corrected before it's tried, and the guarding has grown bigger than the thing being guarded. Anyone standing near it can feel the grip. The practice is carrying more of your worry than of itself.

Get one of those worries onto a single page and follow it. Lay the facts out in plain order, no mood in the lines, and then do the next thing the facts actually ask — not the whole campaign against what might go wrong. Inquiry is your way back here, not more holding. Once it's written out, you'll see which fears are just the future being imagined. The ones that are real are few, and they can be handled one at a time, at the speed they arrive.

cells.tense: You have been standing at the door of your own tradition for a while now.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Pick the smallest piece of this culture you've stepped away from — one meal, one evening — and carry it out once, solidly, as if you meant it.
cells.core:
Something in the shared thing went quiet for you, and you haven't picked it back up. You watch it continue without you, know the words and the shape of it, and take no part. The strength to hold it is still in you — you could do it in your sleep — but nothing is being carried, and the distance feels like it happened to you rather than like something you chose.

Don't try to want the whole tradition back. Lay one step, the one you can see. Choose the smallest piece you can do with your own hands — one meal, one evening, one practice — and do only that one, solidly, the way you'd do a thing you meant. Being able to carry something returns through the doing, not through deciding to care again. One piece done for real tells you whether the rest still fits, and you'll know from there.

cells.tense: What gets kept alive here is your work, and you tell it as if it just happened.
cells.act: apprentice yourself to the material thing
cells.ask: Sit down as a beginner with one piece of this practice, under someone or something that knows it better than you do now.
cells.core:
The customs people keep and pass on here hold because you keep making them hold. You arrange who learns what, remember what matters, keep the thing going through changes most people aren't tracking. Your account of it is that it simply continues. The ones who receive it don't know to say otherwise, and there's nobody else in a position to notice.

Go back to the beginning of it. Before you were the one keeping this alive, you were someone learning it, and something in you liked being shown how — the grip of it in your hands, the plain surprise of it working. Take one piece of the practice and learn it again as a beginner, slowly, from a person or a craft that knows it better than you do now. That's where the whole thing came from. Learn like that for a while, and you'll feel the size of what you've been holding up.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that culture-work here involves other people at all: culture is shared meaning, so the cells render it as customs and practices carried by a group, not as a body of people to be met, and the reader could rightly say 'no, this is my writing/teaching practice alone.' The asks survive either way — tending a small practice, laying out the facts at a table, building one small thing that lasts, apprenticing to it — none of them needs another person on hand. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'the inheritance is already yours to give'; it flatters the seat, and I have cut it.
